newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnians to vote in critical post-war poll.
newsitem.headline: Bosnians to vote in critical post-war poll.

text.p: More than 4,000 polling stations across Bosnia will open at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT) on Saturday for critical post-war elections widely seen as the turning point in the country's fortunes.
But only the future will show whether Bosnia will turn back to war or forward to stability and prosperity.

The United States has led a chorus of senior Western officials in publicly proclaiming that the country has no choice but to go through with the elections, however flawed, if it is ever to recover from the 43-month conflict.
The American envoy who beat out the Dayton peace accord, Richard Holbrooke, leads a U.S. presidential delegation observing the elections.

Far from ratifying the territorial divisions forged in war, Holbrooke declared that the poll would pave the way for the next stage in the peace process -- the creation of central government structures.

"The Dayton agreement does not provide for secession. We are opposed to that and we all agree that that is not what this election is all about," he told reporters after a meeting with Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic.

But secession has been a consistent theme of the campaign for the leading Serb and Croat parties. The ruling Serb Democratic Party (SDS) in particular has made no secret of its desire to cut its territory away from Bosnia and graft it to neighbouring Serbia.

Even when election organisers forced her to publicly denounce such rhetoric on local television, acting Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic used her delivery to make it clear she was committed to Bosnia's division.
Before beginning to read, Plavsic told viewers: "I have been given this statement by the OSCE to read out to you." She then put on her glasses and began to read.
"Apology by Dr Biljana Plavsic...

"The Serb Democratic Party, including myself personally, sincerely apologises for statements made during the election campaign which bring into question the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina."
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) which is organising the poll hoped the statement would convince separatist Serbs that unity is inevitable.
But the biggest short-term fear of the international community was of violence between ethnic rivals meeting one another on Saturday in places they once fought over.
Hundreds of thousands of Bosnia's refugees and displaced people were expected to travel deeply pot-holed roads in the journey back to the home towns they fled during the war.

To make sure the mass movement happens peacefuly, the OSCE and the NATO-led peace keeping force have drawn up an elaborate security plan that directs voters along 19 "secure" routes across the ethnic boundary lines.
Almost every one of the 60,000 peacekeepers will be on duty, securing polling stations and crossing points to snuff out any hint of trouble before it flares out of control.

In a final appeal for peace, U.S. Admiral Joseph Lopez, who commands the NATO force, international peace coordinator Carl Bildt, and Robert Frowick, who is overseeing the elections as regional OSCE director, issued a joint statement.

"We urge you all to approach election day with dignity, to consider your own choice carefully, and to know that your vote is a secret vote," they urged Bosnia's Moslems, Serbs and Croats who have scant experience with democracy.
If the former enemies heed that call, the international officials will declare the day a victory for Bosnia.

But no one seems to have any idea if the joint "democratic" institutions the country is voting for will be any more successful at holding Bosnia together than the last ones which never stopped it descending into war.
